question.prompt: The graph of \(y=x^6-10x^5\) \(+29x^4-4x^3+ax^2\) lies above the line \(y=bx+c\) except at three values of \(x,\) where the graph and the line intersect. What is the largest of those values?

solutions.explanation:
Subtract the line from the polynomial and call the difference
\[
P(x)=x^6-10x^5+29x^4-4x^3+ax^2-bx-c.
\]
The condition says \(P(x)\ge0\) for every real \(x\), with exactly three distinct zeros.

Each zero must have even multiplicity. To see why, write \(P(x)=(x-t)^mR(x)\), where \(R(t)\ne0\). The polynomial \(R\) keeps the same sign sufficiently close to \(t\): writing \(x=t+h\), its nonconstant terms become arbitrarily small with \(h\). If \(m\) were odd, the factor \((x-t)^m\) would change sign across \(t\), forcing \(P\) to be negative on one side.

Three distinct zeros therefore require at least six linear factors, counting multiplicity. Since \(P\) has degree six, each zero occurs exactly twice. Its leading coefficient is \(1\), so
\[
P(x)=Q(x)^2
\]
for a monic cubic \(Q(x)=x^3+ux^2+vx+w\).

The leading coefficients determine this cubic without needing \(a,b,c\). Expanding the square gives
\[
Q(x)^2=x^6+2ux^5+(u^2+2v)x^4
+(2w+2uv)x^3+\cdots.
\]
Matching the displayed coefficients yields
\[
2u=-10,\qquad u^2+2v=29,
\qquad2w+2uv=-4.
\]
Consequently \(u=-5\), \(v=2\), and \(w=8\). Factoring,
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q(x)&=x^3-5x^2+2x+8\\
&=(x-2)(x^2-3x-4)\\
&=(x-2)(x-4)(x+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the three intersection values are \(-1,2,4\). This factorization also verifies feasibility: choosing \(a=-76\), \(b=-32\), and \(c=-64\) makes the difference exactly this square, positive away from those three values. The largest is \(\boxed{4}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutions.title: Use nonnegativity to identify a polynomial square
Stationary polynomial zeros and repeated factor division
